chapters.summary: Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez welcomes attendees to the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education hearing. She frames New York City as linguistically diverse and notes that 45% of young children in New York State are multilingual learners.
chapters.title: Chair Gutiérrez opens hearing on multilingual early childhood education

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez, Chair of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, and welcome to today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Double special welcome to the incoming DC for our hearing today, supporting multi-language learners and early childhood education programs.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: New York City is widely recognized as the most linguistically diverse city in the world.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Shout out to Queens.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez says multilingual early childhood education supports cognitive development, cultural identity, and emotional regulation. She cites a 2025 study finding too few bilingual pre-K programs for the city's multilingual learners.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez cites benefits of home-language instruction and bilingual pre-K shortage

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: In New York State, the proportion of multilingual young children is higher than the national average of 32%, with approximately 45% of young children ages 0 to 5 in New York identifying as multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Access to multilingual early childhood education serves as a critical cornerstone for both cognitive development and social equity.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Nurturing children's home languages develops their positive sense of self and cultural identity.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It also maintains strong ties with family and community and supports young children's social behavioral

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: and emotional regulation.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Research shows a clear relationship between the age of exposure to a language and a child's success in learning that language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yet, a 2025 study of New York City's pre-kindergarten program found that there are not nearly enough designated bilingual pre-K programs available to support the growing number of multi-language learners.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez notes President Trump's executive order designating English as the official U.S. language. She condemns the proposed English-only instruction rule for Head Start and calls for the city to step up multilingual services.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez criticizes federal English-only Head Start proposal

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Last year, President Trump issued an executive order designating English as the official language of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And about a month ago, his administration released a notice of proposed rulemaking proposing an English-only instruction requirement in all Head Start programs.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Boo.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: With the persistent federal attacks on multilingual services, now is the time for the city to step up its commitment to all of its residents in providing these services, including to our youngest learners.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez lists questions about how the administration supports multilingual early childhood students, expands programs, and informs families. She also introduces Resolution 650 opposing the federal Head Start rule change.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez outlines hearing questions and Resolution 650

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So today we'll ask the administration how you are supporting supporting how are you supporting multilingual early childhood education students across our city?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you planning to expand multilingual supports as the early childhood education system grows?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How are you informing multilingual families about their early childhood education options?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We will also hear Rezo 650 sponsored by myself opposing the federal

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: opposing the federally proposed rule change titled Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs and calling on the federal government to prioritize protecting and growing access to high-quality education for young children.

utterances.text: I want to thank the members of Early Childhood Education, our subcommittee, who've joined us today, Council Member Rita.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Joseph and Councilmember Simka Felder and online council member.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We're all here today.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Simca.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And additionally, I want to thank the staff of our committee, Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham, Katie Salina, Grace Amato, and Julene Lawless and Margaret Barnsley, as well as my own staff, Frank Hulka, Angelica Colon, and our outgoing Fela Elalau for their work on today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And finally, thank you to everyone who's signed up to testify.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from you.

chapters.summary: Emmy Liss, Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education, introduces the administration's universal child care vision. She says multilingual learner support is central to that goal.
chapters.title: Emmy Liss presents Mayor's Office vision for universal child care

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez and members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: My name is Emmy Liss, and I am the Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I am joined today by my colleagues from New York City Public Schools, and we would like to thank you for convening this important hearing and for giving us the opportunity to testify before you.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The Mamdani administration is committed to a vision of universal child care, a city in which every child under five has access to free, high-quality early care and education

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: offered in a range of culturally competent settings with caregivers and educators who are trained, respected, and fairly compensated.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Supporting multilingual learners is a critical component of the mayor's goal because we know that child care cannot be universal in one of the most diverse cities in the world unless we support multilingual learners and providers.

chapters.summary: Liss argues all children deserve early learning that honors their heritage and home language. She shares her son's experience in a Spanish dual-language pre-K program.
chapters.title: Emmy Liss says multilingual programs benefit all children

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: All children deserve access to rich early learning environments that honor and celebrate their heritage and support their growth, no matter what language they speak at home.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are also blessed as a city with thousands of early childhood educators who speak languages other than English in their classrooms and programs, allowing children of all backgrounds to feel a sense of belonging and to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Creating early childhood education environments that support and encourage multilingual learning benefits all children.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I know this from research and evidence.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I also share this from experience.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Last year, my son was enrolled in one of the city's pre-K Spanish dual language programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: As a child coming from an English-speaking home, he had a chance to learn with and from his peers who came from Spanish-speaking homes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I saw the ways in which the children learned from each other and saw each other's language skills as an asset and a strength.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: All of the parents in the classroom were able to engage with the educators and with the day-to-day lessons, regardless of which language we spoke at home.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I know the benefits that I saw are not unique to my son's experience alone and represent what many families and educators experience every day.

chapters.summary: Liss describes collaboration with NYC Public Schools' Division of Early Childhood Education. She introduces Erica Phillips as the new Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education.
chapters.title: Emmy Liss introduces Deputy Chancellor Erica Phillips

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Together with our partners at the New York City Public Schools Division of Early Childhood Education, the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education has been working closely on a number of initiatives and programs

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: toward the goal of delivering free, high-quality care and education for every child under five in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I'm thrilled to introduce my newest colleague, Erica Phillips, who recently joined the division as the new Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Deputy Chancellor Phillips brings decades of experience in early childhood education and has worked closely with child care providers who are serving multilingual children.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: She will now share more background on the work that the Division of Early Childhood Education is doing to support multilingual learners, and we look forward to then taking your questions.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Erica Phillips introduces herself as Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education and names her colleagues. She describes more than 20 years of experience in early childhood, K-12, nonprofit, and family child care leadership.
chapters.title: Erica Phillips introduces herself and NYCPS early childhood team

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez and members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: My name is Erica Phillips, and I serve as the Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education at New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I am joined today by Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Georgette Branch, Chief of Learning and Partnerships, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Brenda Garcia, Chief of the Office of Multilingual Learners, and Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Arabelle L.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Pembroke, Senior Director of Inclusion and Support for Emergent Multilingual Learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to be here and for your continued partnership in supporting New York City's youngest learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I come to this role with more than 20 years of experience across early childhood and K-12 education, business, and nonprofit leadership.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Much of my career is focused on building systems that support young children and families while assisting the educators and caregivers who serve them.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Before joining New York City Public Schools, I served as the executive director of the National Association for Family Child Care,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: where I worked at the federal level to strengthen early learning programs, advance child care policies, and elevate the voices of the early educators and providers who have served as the backbone of the early childhood system.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Previously, I spent eight years at All Our Kin, an early childhood organization focused on supporting home-based child care providers, where I helped to bring its family child care network to New York City.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: This work is deeply personal to me as the daughter and granddaughter of early educators and caregivers.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I am honored to bring those experiences.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: to New York City public schools and to lead our work to strengthen early care and education for children and families across New York City.

chapters.summary: Phillips says New York City children enter early childhood programs with linguistic and cultural assets. She says the system should recognize those languages as strengths and give families meaningful access.
chapters.title: Phillips outlines an assets-based approach to emergent multilingual learners

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss how we support emergent multilingual children and families across early childhood programs in New York City, as well as our early childhood dual language bilingual education program.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: New York City's children enter our early childhood programs with tremendous linguistic and cultural assets.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Across our early childhood system, children may be learning English while also developing one of the many other languages spoken by New York City families.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our responsibility is to build an early childhood system that recognizes those languages as strengths,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: provides children with developmentally appropriate opportunities to learn across languages, and ensures that families have meaningful access to their children's education.

chapters.summary: Phillips contrasts K-12 English language learner identification under Part 154 with early childhood identification. She describes the state's Emergent Multilingual Learner Language Profile, a family survey available in 24 languages.
chapters.title: Phillips explains ECE identification of emergent multilingual learners

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The process for identifying emergent multilingual learners in early childhood differs from the process used to identify English language learners in K-12 schools.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Under Commissioner's Regulation Part 154, K-12 schools follow a formal process for identifying English language learners, including the home language questionnaire,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: an individual interview when appropriate, and the New York State Identification Test for English Language Learners, NISATL.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: An English language proficiency assessment.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Those requirements do not apply in the same way in early childhood settings, where children are identified as emergent multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: learners based on information families provide about their child's language, background, and experiences.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: New York State uses the Emergent Multilingual Learner Language Profile, a family-completed survey available in 24 languages that asks which languages are spoken by parents and caregivers.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Which languages the child understands and uses, and the family's preferred language for program communication.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The purpose is not to measure English proficiency, but to identify children whose home or primary language is other than English to help programs plan linguistically responsive instruction and supports.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Across early childhood settings, multilingualism is treated as an asset.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: All programs are required to support multilingual learners by using developmentally appropriate practices such as visual aids, modeling, intentional vocabulary development,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: home language connections, family partnerships, and culturally and linguistic responsive instruction.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The goal is to enable all children to fully participate in learning while also developing English.

chapters.summary: Phillips says all early childhood programs must use visual aids, modeling, vocabulary development, home language connections, and family partnerships. She says these practices help children participate while developing English.
chapters.title: Phillips details instructional supports for multilingual learners

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Emergent multilingual learners across early childhood settings experience language-rich, culturally and linguistic responsive learning experiences.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our emergent multilingual guidance, as well as ongoing city professional learning,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: supports educators with instructional strategies.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Those include using children's home languages and linguistic strengths, visuals and real objects, gestures,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: intentional vocabulary development, repeated readings, family knowledge, and developmentally appropriate observation across languages and communication modalities.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: As reflected in the New York State Education Department's blueprint for MLELL success, we believe all teachers are teachers of multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Every educator can create an environment in which children's languages are visible, valued, and incorporated meaningfully into learning.

chapters.summary: Phillips distinguishes dual-language bilingual education as one model from the broader responsibility to support emergent multilingual learners. She says every educator can make children's languages visible and valued.
chapters.title: Phillips says all educators share responsibility for multilingual learners

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: These distinctions matter because while dual language bilingual education is a specific program model, the responsibility for supporting emergent multilingual learners belongs to the entire early childhood ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The Department of Early Childhood Education works in partnership with the Office of Multilingual Learners to align this work within the broader NYCPS guidance and resources for multilingual learners,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: while ensuring that supports reflect the particular needs of young children in early childhood settings.

chapters.summary: Phillips says a child can be both an emergent multilingual learner and have a disability. She calls for coordinated language, communication, learning, and disability supports, including for children with IEPs.
chapters.title: Phillips addresses multilingual learners with disabilities

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Multilingualism intersects with other areas of a child's development.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: A child can be an emergent multilingual learner and also have a disability.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Supporting that child requires educators and families to consider language development, communication, learning, and disability together.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Language differences should not be mistaken for disability, nor should a disability result in a child's linguistic strengths being overlooked.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: That is why our work to support inclusion in emergent multilingual learners must remain connected.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Educators need dedicated support, family partnership, and multiple sources of information to understand how a child communicates and learns across languages and settings.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: In practice, this means providing multiple ways for children to access instruction and demonstrate understanding.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Educators can pair spoken language with visuals, gestures, modeling, objectives, and assistive technology.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Intentionally build vocabulary in both English and the child's home language.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Break directions into smaller steps.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Provide repetition and additional processing time.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And use predictable routines that reduce linguistic and cognitive demands.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Small group instruction, peer modeling, and opportunities to respond through speech, movement, pictures, or other communication systems can also support participation.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For children with IEPs, accommodations and specialized supports should be integrated with culturally and linguistically responsive instruction.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: partners in identifying how children communicate, what they understand in their home language, and what strategies are most effective across child settings.

chapters.summary: Phillips says families receive translated enrollment information and interpretation through NYCPS and early childhood programs. She says technology can help but should not replace human translation for important decisions.
chapters.title: Phillips describes family engagement and language access

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Families are essential partners in the education of emergent multilingual learners across diverse early childhood settings that we support, including our dual language bilingual education programs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: During enrollment, families have access to translated information, and programs may use multilingual staff, interpretation resources, and appropriate translation technology to communicate with families.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: NYCPS also provides families with broader language access supports, including written translation and in-person,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: virtual, and over-the-phone interpretation services.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Families can access interpretation in many languages, and early childhood communications and enrollment resources are available in multiple languages.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Additionally, center-based settings and family child care networks have access to over-the-phone interpretation services and translation templates,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: to support direct communication with families, whether in person or by the phone.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For family child care providers, the Affiliated Family Child Care Network is responsible for ensuring providers can communicate with families and connect them to interpretation and translation resources.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our work is to strengthen consistency across the system so that a family's ability to communicate with their child's program does not depend solely on the language skills of individual staff members.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Technology can support that work, but it should not replace high-quality human translation and interpretation, particularly when families are making important decisions about enrollment, instruction, special education, or other services.

chapters.summary: Phillips says the early childhood dual language model provides instruction in English and a partner language. She reports 99 verified sites with Spanish, Mandarin, Russian, French, Italian, Polish, Korean, and Arabic.
chapters.title: Phillips presents dual language bilingual education model and sites

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The Early Childhood Dual Language Bilingual Education Program model provides instruction in English and a partner language across district schools, pre-K centers, and contracted community-based early childhood programs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We have 99 verified dual language bilingual education program sites across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Partner languages represented across these programs include Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Russian, French, Italian, Polish, Korean, and Arabic.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Dual language programming is an important component of how New York City Public Schools supports multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Across our early childhood system, programs provide language supports that may include bilingual or multilingual staff,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: translated family communications, interpretation at family meetings, and instructional practices that support the continued development of both English and a child's home language.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: An early childhood dual language bilingual education program is not automatically established when a particular number of children who speak one language are enrolled.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thoughtful planning is essential.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: DECE must consider the linguistic profile of enrolled and prospective families, parental interests, staffing, and bilingual educator capacity.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: quality, geography, enrollment sustainability, and opportunities for continuity into elementary school when determining where dual language bilingual education programs can be established and sustained.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The strength of any dual language program depends heavily on its educators.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Early childhood dual language bilingual education programs require appropriately credentialed bilingual educators,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: and we recognize that the available pool of bilingual certified early childhood teachers is more limited than the general early childhood workforce.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: New York State and NYCPS support pathways for educators to obtain bilingual extensions.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Strengthening that pipeline remains important as we consider future expansion.

chapters.summary: Phillips lists data sources used to plan supports and identify gaps. She names priorities including data-driven professional learning, bilingual educator pipeline, implementation support, and family language access.
chapters.title: Phillips outlines data and future priorities for multilingual learners

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Furthermore, across all early childhood settings, we believe every educator can create environments that support emergent multilingual leaders, instructional coordinators, education administrators,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: and other members of DECE's instructional support structure work within programs on curriculum, instructional practice, professional learning, and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The ECE has access to several important sources of information, including home language information, enrollment data, the early childhood emergent multilingual learner profile,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: my school's information, teaching strategies gold, provider information.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Current dual language bilingual education program locations.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: and languages, and K-12 bilingual education program data.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: These data provide an increasingly strong foundation for planning.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our goal is to continue strengthening our data infrastructure so we can better understand where emergent multilingual learners are being served,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: what languages are being represented, where opportunities may be limited, and how program quality and access can improve over time.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Looking ahead, our work to support emergent multilingual learners is focused on several priorities.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: First is using data to identify potential gaps in foreign professional learning cycles and build educator capacity.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The second is strengthening the bilingual educator pipeline while continuing to build the capacity of all early childhood educators to support multilingual children.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The third is to strengthen implementation support to enhance the quality of children's learning experiences.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And the fourth is to ensure families have meaningful language access and a clear voice in determining which programs best meet the needs of their children.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Our goal this year is to build sustainable, high-quality programs in the communities where children and families need them, while ensuring that every multilingual learner across our early childhood system is supported,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: whether or not that child attends a designated dual-language bilingual education program.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We appreciate the subcommittee's attention to this work and the council's continued partnership on behalf of New York City's youngest learners and families.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: to testify today, and I look forward to your questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Chancellor.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I also want to acknowledge committee member Kevin Riley, who joined us.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you both for your very thoughtful testimonies.

utterances.text: And I just want to start by saying my child is also in a dual language program and was able to participate in the pre-K class as like an introduction.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And that's what really kind of exposed me to understanding the value of this program as early as four and even younger.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So thank you for this testimony, DC.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how the DOE defines multilingual learner and how it differs from K-12. Georgette Branch describes emergent multilingual learners as children from homes speaking a language other than English, while Brenda Garcia explains the K-12 umbrella term and program models.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks how NYCPS defines multilingual learner

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I wanted to ask, just to start.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You got something for me?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You got to go.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I do love the open transparency.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you just start, can you define, and I graduated public schools here.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think when I went to school, it was.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What was the name of the class?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It was just like the bilingual.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: ESL.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I know that the vocabulary and the languages have changed.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So can you just share with me how the DOE defines multi-language learner?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Yes, so we are thinking very expansively about how we're supporting multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And to frame it, the way that we view that for the early childhood is a little bit different than how we view English language learners in K-12.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask my colleague, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Branch, to provide some detail on how we define our multilingual learners for early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And then Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Garcia can.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Share what it looks like in K-12.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So in early childhood education, the way that we define our emergent multilingual learners is students who come from a home that supports, you know, that speaks a language other than English.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So essentially families self-identify and they tell us that, you know, their little one speaks Spanish or is learning to speak Spanish or another language in addition to English.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So that's the definition.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And what is the, thank you, that seems easy enough.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What is the definition?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How is it different from then K through 12 or 1 through 12?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So the state introduced the term multilingual learner.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And so it's an umbrella term.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Multilingual learner includes English language learners, which I'll define in a minute, former English language learners.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So those are kids who are L's at some point.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And it also includes any student who is learning a new language.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So that virtually could be any student in our system taking a world language course or heritage language course.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Our English language learners are the students who actually are entitled, as per CR Part 154, to English language.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: English language acquisition instructions.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So it used to be called English as a second language.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Now it's called English as a new language or transitional bilingual education programs or dual language bilingual education programs.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Those are the three program models.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether the early childhood definition is appropriate long-term and whether framing changes for infants versus pre-K students. Branch says the family-informed approach will continue and applies across ages.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks if ECE definition will remain appropriate across ages

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Wow.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I know it's a little, it's obviously different for early childhood education, but what you shared seems simple.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: This seems a little more nuanced.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there any plan?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like, does this feel like the appropriate definition for early childhood?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For the foreseeable future.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And I believe it is the most appropriate because,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: All of our students are emergent learners, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: They're emergent language learners.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Some of our students, they come in with very little language, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Initially, they're coming in as early as six months.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we're really looking to the families to share information in terms of what they see as the best approach and utilize that to also honor that in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So for the time and the foreseeable future, that will...

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Continue to be how we define our emergent language learners in early childhood education.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And does the framing of the question change for a six-month, like the parent of a six-month-old, two-year-old, three-year-old versus a pre-K student where

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: maybe they have more language and you're asking more about the parent, you know, at six months or two-year-old versus the four-year-old?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Does that framing change or is it?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It's consistent because at the, pretty much at home, whatever language

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: is introduced at home, whether it's the parent's language or maybe grandma comes over and speaks an additional language, we're really using that information to determine how to best support the child in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So it may not even just be that it's a French-speaking household, but maybe, you know, there's grandparents or individuals who come over who speak Spanish as well.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And if the family shares that information with us and, you know, the hope and desire is that the language acquisition is advanced across all of those languages.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We support that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks if NYCPS or the Mayor's Office have an estimated number of multilingual learners in early childhood programs. Branch reports 30,058 total, with breakdowns for pre-K, 3K, 2K, and infants.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks for number of multilingual learners in ECE

utterances.text: My next question is just regarding data for early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I know that it might be a little bit more complicated, but does NYCPS or the Mayor's Office of Child Care, do you all have an estimated number of multilingual learners in early childhood education programs?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So currently we have across the entire portfolio, so across all of our pre-K centers, 3K,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: our 2K expansion programs, and our infants, we have a total of 30,058 multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So I can give you the breakdown if you want in terms of like pre-K versus 3K, 2K.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Would you like that?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you just repeat then?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You said 30,000?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So the total is 30,058.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Wow, that's precise.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm pleased if you could do the breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So in pre-K, we have 12,725.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: In our 2K programs, 581.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And our little infants, 15 currently.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then how do you all, how do you kind of keep, how do you keep track of this?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's like, how often are you being informed of like,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: There's a new family who was identified as like a multi-language learner.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So initially, the, you know, initially families can actually share that information.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: even when they apply, right, when they're applying through the MySchools account.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But that information is also maintained at the school or at the program.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And that information is shared with the division.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And we're able to keep track of that because in addition to just the numbers and knowing that we have them, we do a lot of coaching.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: The Division of Early Childhood Education, that's really...

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: What I'm most proud of is in terms of how we really are able to support programs and really go in and provide support to teachers so that they can better support their multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So that information is captured and sent over to the division quite often.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We have people on the ground who are able to also keep track of that information as well.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether families' language information changes during the school year. Branch says new students may arrive but families rarely change their reported home language.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks whether multilingual learner data changes mid-year

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you find that it will change in the middle of the school year?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Maybe you're a family who, like, just didn't respond in the same way for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you find that that happens often where maybe in the middle of the school year they're like, actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It's not typically that it changes for the families, but we may get new students, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So now we have additional multilingual learners in the program.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But it's not usually the case that we have a family.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Who says little Johnny is a multilingual learner.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: He speaks French at home.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And now that's no longer the case.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: No, I think of the reverse, where I think the way that you defined it earlier could be like, maybe abuela comes over once in a while, and now my child is being exposed in a way that maybe the parents didn't.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So that's kind of what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That's not typical.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: I would say that.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It happens from time to time.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: time to time, but I think it's inconsequential in terms of how often we take a trip and we absorb a whole lot.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether the multilingual learner counts are current 2026-2027 enrollment or last year's data. Branch says the numbers are current as of September 25.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks to clarify enrollment data timing

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm going to ask one more question and then I'm going to pass it off to Councilmember Ray.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, sure.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, can you just clarify the numbers that you just shared for multilingual learners?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's the current enrollment, 2026, 2027, or for last year?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That is our, I believe that's our current enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As of September 25th.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, wow.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: My next question before I pass it off to Councilmember Riley.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether families whose primary language is not English face limits in applying to 3K, pre-K, or 2K programs. Erica Phillips says demand is strong and over 80% of families received one of their top choices.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks whether home language limits program access

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you all, have you all found that if a family wants a seat in 3K or pre-K or now or 2K

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: and they want a seat in a particular program and it's from a family whose primary language is a language other than English, have you found that that raises any limitations for what schools they attend or even apply to?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Or is that a question that you pose to families?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So we are very actively looking at what families need, both based on the language of the family and really demand around all of the programs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And that's something that we've been monitoring quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: There is really strong demand for the dual language program from families who speak a language other than English and also for families who want to expose their child to another language.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And, you know, so yes, we do have, you know, a lot of interest in that and making sure that we are prioritizing.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So our goal for classes are for them to be 50-50 native, the language of that program.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Families who speak another language.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And so we are able to meet families'needs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I think over 80% of families were able to get one of their top schools, including, you know, dual language, if that was one of the ones that they prioritized.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: There are options and ways that we need to continue to monitor what the demand is.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: But we are able to prioritize families who need that dual language program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is the strong demand that you mentioned, is that particularly for pre-K or is it a mix of like?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Families are in 3K.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The strong demand that I was talking about was for our dual language program specifically.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It could be K-12.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It could be K-12, but specifically thinking about pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And we just, for the first time, opened up two 3K dual language programs this year.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Where are those programs?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We will have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I will pass it to Councilmember Riley.

chapters.summary: Kevin Riley asks how many DOE and contracted early childhood programs offer dual language or enhanced language supports, including by borough, language, and seat count. Phillips and Branch describe 99 dual-language sites and explain enhanced language supports.
chapters.title: Riley asks about dual-language and enhanced language program availability

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Chancellor, and to the panel that came out here today for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We truly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: My question is going to be surrounded around program models and access.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the DOE offers the dual language and enhanced language support programs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The dual language programs teach English and target languages.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So does the DOE and contracted early childhood programs, how many, excuse me, how many DOE and contracted early childhood programs currently offer dual language or enhanced language?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And do you have that by borough, language, and seat count?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: First, I'll talk a little bit about what we've been talking about, the dual language piece and the enhanced language and how we think about that.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And then I'll turn it over to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Pembroke to provide some of the detail about the specific programs that we have.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So dual language programs, we have 99 of those, and they're very specific of the different languages.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The enhanced language supports is a designation within my schools that indicates that a school is able to, you know, offer supports and resources.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: But in reality, on the ground, we actually expect all schools to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And so the enhanced language supports, you know, we believe that all of the schools have the resources and the expectations to be able to meet any multilingual child that comes into the program.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So I will turn it over.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: To Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Branch, you're going to take that question.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That one.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: I just wanted to also just offer a little bit more in terms of the explanation of the enhanced language supports, because we see it on my schools.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: You know, I saw it even before I came to the division and always wondered what it really meant.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And what it truly means is that a family can go to a program and there's someone there who speaks their home language, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That person could be a lead teacher, a teacher's assistant.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It could be a custodial staff.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It could be a secretary, any individual.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It is not an instructional program, though.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That's what's important to note.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So that it's not...

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Similar or on the same continuum as dual language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: It's literally about language access.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And what you just heard in terms of what DC Phillips shared is that that's the expectation of all of our programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So not only enhanced language programs, but the expectation is that supports are being provided in a family's home language at each and every one of our programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So that's actually expanded beyond the enhanced language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: In terms of the breakdown,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Don't have it by district, but I can give you specifically how many programs in pre-K, 3K, and what the languages are, if that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay, so in terms of pre-K programs, we have five programs that support Mandarin Chinese exclusively.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We have one program that supports Mandarin Chinese and Arabic, so you'll find both languages in that program.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We have two programs that support Chinese, Mandarin, and Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Again, you'll find both in those programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We have two programs, two French dual language programs, one Italian,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: one Korean, one Polish, two Russian, one program that has Russian and Spanish, and 77 Spanish dual language programs in pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is all early childhood?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: All.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Early childhood, the littles.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: For 3K, you know, we're very, very excited about the two new 3K programs that we opened this year.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And right now, the 3K programs, they support Russian, one.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: One supports Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So those are the two.

chapters.summary: Riley asks how the city determines which languages to prioritize when expanding multilingual programs. Branch cites community demand, seat availability, geography, and family language access as factors.
chapters.title: Riley asks how NYC prioritizes languages and access barriers

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And how does the city determine which languages to prioritize when creating or expanding multilingual programs?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we want to make it accessible to all families, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we prioritize based on the community demand.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We prioritize based on seat availability.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And we also consider what the geographic location of the needs are.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: When we consider opening a dual language program, we take a look at those different factors to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But ultimately, our goal is always to expand the dual language classroom so that all families have access to that type of model for their multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And could you share any barriers that will prevent any families from accessing these programs that you've seen?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Well, what we will not make sure that we consider are simplifying our family's access to language and language support.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So what we currently have in place now are our opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: for the application to be available in the 13 languages that support the 99% of students and the languages they speak at home.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: In addition to that, we consider what would be

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: what would be critical family-facing communications.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we have our internal unit that supports that work.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Our interpretation and our translation unit helps to subsidize some of those resources for us.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And we also have partner vendors that take care of that work for our CBOs and our family child care networks.

chapters.summary: Riley asks how many early childhood educators are qualified to teach or support each language. Branch says 108 3K and pre-K dual-language licensed teachers, and Brenda Garcia adds state professional learning requirements.
chapters.title: Riley asks about bilingual early childhood educator workforce

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Chair, may I ask a few more?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just wanted to go into workforce, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So we all know that educators are needed within these specific departments so they can help educate our children.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How many early childhood educators in the DOE and contracted programs are qualified to teach in or support each language used by enrolled children?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay, so in terms of just multilingual learners, again, in the Division of Early Childhood Education, all of our teachers are equipped to support multilingual learners because all of our kids are emerging language learners.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But specifically for dual language, we have 108.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Teachers who are certified, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And they are lead teachers in classrooms across our city.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So 108 3K and pre-K dual language licensed teachers.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: with the birth to two certificate or they're on a pathway and very close to receiving the birth to two certification.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And lastly, you said everyone's equipped.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So can you just explain that a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there professional development?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there compensation for educators if they want to get a little bit more training?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you just explain that a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So in early childhood education, we have a robust ecosystem of support, specifically in learning and partnerships.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That's one of the verticals, as well as capacity building and family engagement.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We have what we call instructional coordinators, and they're actual coaches that go into programs, and they work with teachers side by side.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So they're able to provide them specific feedback on the spot that they can utilize today, not next week, but actually today.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And they're providing supports around literacy, but also around, you know, really utilizing the home language and how to have that come alive in the classroom on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We also have social workers who go into programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Again, our staff, they are field-based.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And they support the social-emotional learning aspect and help teachers to ensure that they're tapping into, you know, culturally and linguistic approaches each and every day in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We even have what we call inclusion specialists.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And their job is on top of the layers of support that I just named.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: If we have programs where individuals are saying, I need a little bit more support, they are certified teachers who are certified

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: in special education or bilingual education, and they go in to ensure that there are inclusive practices so that everyone, when we say all, we mean all, will have access to the curriculum, have access to a learning environment.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Across our programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And of course we have PL, we offer ongoing professional learning in person, we offer some sessions hybrid,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: some sessions online, but what I'm most proud of is really that job embedded, that on the ground support where you can get feedback automatically and improve your practice the very next day.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just going to add another piece to the requirement of professional learning specific to multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So New York State Ed requires 15% of all the continuing teacher and leader professional learning to be focused on multilingual learners for any teacher or leader to maintain their certification.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So that's one way in which we ensure every person who is certified to teach in the system has at least 15% of their PL going to that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And then any teacher who's either English as a new language or bilingual certified, they're required 50% of that CTLE to be specific to multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So that's.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: just another way for us to ensure that teachers are supported to support our really diverse, linguistically and culturally diverse populations.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether dual-language programs hold designated seats for children whose primary language is not English. Emmy Liss says programs aim for 50% target-language and 50% non-target-language seats, with waitlists possible.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about dual-language lottery seats and waitlists

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I also want to acknowledge you've been joined by committee member, Councilmember Gail Brewer and Councilmember Julie Wan online.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a couple more questions and then pass it over to, oh no, not a lantern fly, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Save us.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Goodness.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I had a question about, somebody will save us.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I had a question about families who want to see it in, let's say, an existing pre-K dual language program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I guess, is there designated seats in the lottery for children for these programs whose primary language is a language other than English for these dual language programs?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there like a certain amount of seats?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So by design, dual language programs, those that specifically are teaching in that format, are meant to have

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: 50% of children coming from a household that speaks the target language and 50% of children who are coming from a household that does not speak the target language.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so in the admissions process, essentially 50% of the seats are held for each group.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so a family does indicate when they apply on my schools whether or not they speak that language at home.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you have a sense, are there instances where there are waiting lists for the 50% of those families who speak that language versus the 50% who don't?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Just as with any early childhood program, there may be waiting lists.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: When a family applies for 3K or pre-K, they can list essentially an unlimited number of programs on their application.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And any program that they ranked higher than the program they are ultimately offered a spot at, they are automatically placed on the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So a family may have ranked five dual language programs, for example, and gotten into their fourth choice.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So they would then be on the wait list for those three that they ranked higher.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Or similarly, a parent who ranked a mix of dual language and non-dual language programs, they would have any of the programs ranked higher than their admitted choice.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: They'd automatically be placed on a wait list.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether dual-language pre-K seats correspond to kindergarten seats. Liss and Garcia say the city seeks continuity but does not explicitly reserve every pre-K seat for kindergarten.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about pre-K to kindergarten dual-language continuity

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you all have a sense of there is, is there an exact amount of kindergarten through five seats or maybe kindergarten seats for that dual language, for the amount of like dual language in the pre-K?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For example, if there's 22 slots in dual language pre-K, is it expected that there will be 22 slots in kindergarten or potentially more, but not less?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I'll just say as a value, I know the Deputy Chancellor mentioned this when planning, we do look for opportunities to create continuity so that children can have an experience in K-12 education that builds on their early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But I'll turn it to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Garcia for that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: That's something that's really important to us.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: of all students in K-12 report a home language other than English.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And so we do believe that when kids are just like you experienced, exposed to dual language, multilingual education in the early years, being able to establish that foundation and continuing kindergarten is fundamental.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So we work really closely with the Division of Early Childhood Education on

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: and the community on ensuring that we have a pattern to be able to grow the seats for students who are in pre-K in dual language programs and have them be able to continue in kindergarten.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks what happens to families in non-NYCPS dual-language or immersion programs seeking kindergarten seats. Liss says kindergarten capacity aims to serve both articulating pre-K students and other community children with language needs.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about non-NYCPS pre-K families and kindergarten slots

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And are there scenarios where families are not enrolled in a NYCPS pre-K program, but

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: in some kind of kind of dual language or immersion program, and then they may not have a slot in kindergarten just because you're reserving those for the pre-K students?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, they are not explicitly reserved exactly for the reason you just said.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Every school has a different student population for pre-K versus kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There may be families who change schools between pre-K and kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There may be families who were in pre-K at a community-based program and are coming in for kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But the goal is to have sufficient capacity in kindergarten to be able to support children who are articulating from pre-K to K, as well as children who may be coming from within the community and similarly have a language need.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And I think that the other piece is that

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Once a child comes into kindergarten and goes through the formal identification process, if they are an English language learner, the parent comes in for a parent orientation, and they are entitled

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: to choose between English as a new language, dual language, or transitional bilingual education.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Starting kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So if the school doesn't offer it, they can request a transfer to a school nearby.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: That does offer the program model that they prefer.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks when families learn about kindergarten bilingual program options. Garcia says identification can begin June 1 for pre-K students, but orientation generally occurs in the first 10 days of school.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez questions timing of kindergarten language identification

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is that communicated to the families any sooner?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: It's communicated once the orientation happens.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So it's the first 10 days of school generally.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's a little tough.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's a little, I mean.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The idea that like parents are engaging with like that school leadership team well before orientation is ideal.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But I feel like there are scenarios where parents kind of walk into this and not realize that until once they've already made arrangements for like their kid to go to that school.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Well, what's distinct for the pre-K students is that a school can start the identification process on June 1st of the year before.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So if a parent comes in and they register, they can start that orientation process.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How will they know to do that?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: It automatically happens.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Like all K-12 schools are trained to administer the home language identification survey to begin with.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And then if, you know, a home language other than English is reported, then they administer the NICETEL.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And then automatically from there, they get the orientation.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Shannon can choose.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you have a way of checking in with individual schools and school districts to make sure that that is happening as early as June?
