utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, we have many ways.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So we do announce that in our P weekly, which is the weekly email that goes to all principals when that window is open so they can begin identification.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And then we have systems and processes in place.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So every school has a CEP, right, comprehensive education plan.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Within that plan, there's a language allocation policy.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And there we request for schools to have a plan on how they're going to ensure the identification of students, including students who are coming from pre-K and entering kindergarten beginning June 1st.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it to Councilmember Brew for her questions.

chapters.summary: Gale Brewer asks how students can continue a language like Russian beyond early childhood when District 3 lacks pathways. Garcia describes bilingual revitalization efforts and an Italian expansion in District 15.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about language continuity and expanding programs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been listening online, so I heard all these great discussions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, I have some who managed to get from early childhood all the way through middle school French, but not Russian.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, they'd have early childhood Russian, then they have elementary, but not beyond that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So is that really possible to continue the language?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it's not possible in School District 3.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how do you make that happen?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or other languages, you know.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: I could speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So that's something that we're really committed to.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And ensuring that there's continuity from pre-K to 12 and that students graduate with a New York State seal of biliteracy ultimately.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We work really closely with superintendents in the community.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So, for example, in a situation where we have a middle school and community is looking for a feeder, right, to go to high school, we work closely with superintendents.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We have with superintendents and principals in the community.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Our office specifically has been able to provide a school allocation memorandum over the past four years for the revitalization of bilingual programs, which includes a planning year for schools opening up a bilingual program.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And we use the data to inform that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So that has been a very specific focus of ours.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: For example, we've been able to expand in District 15 this year, it's continuity for Italian.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So we can now say we have pre-K Italian, we have elementary Italian, and this year we'll have middle school Italian.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: That's just one example, right?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And so it's something, again, we look at the data, we look at the patterns,

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: we take in community input, and then we work with superintendents and principals and then have them participate in our bilingual revitalization efforts, which means that the school gets professional learning for a year on how to plan for the

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: program, on how to hire teachers, on curriculum, on all of the pieces that will lead to a sustainable program.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Because that is like a key piece, is a program that's going to open and it's going to stand the test of time, not close within a year or two.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether there are enough teachers in different languages and how the city recruits them. Liss, Phillips, and Branch describe outreach to multilingual communities, higher education partnerships, and bilingual extensions.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about bilingual teacher shortages and recruitment

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, we'll keep working on the Russian then.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question also is, I know you talked about the teachers and the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have enough teachers in these different languages, or is there a shortage?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that something that is able to be addressed, or is that you've got so many different languages?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I will just say broadly and then turn to my colleagues to speak to some of the particulars.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that as we continue to expand access to early childhood education broadly and specifically to support more and more of our multilingual learners, we cannot do that without investing in the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so as we continue to invest in workforce development for early childhood education,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: we need to continue both bringing multilingual educators into the pipeline and supporting those who are already in our system to get their bilingual extension or otherwise develop the skills to support multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But I'll pass to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how are you doing that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you calling the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, I'm serious.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I mean, I think at a high level, as we think about...

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, how we promote the jobs in early childhood education, doing outreach to diverse communities in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We have so many multilingual speakers in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So making sure that we are reaching them in the communities where they are, partnering with institutions of higher education who are serving a multilingual student population,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: as well as working with existing teachers in our early childhood and K-12 system who want to go back to school and earn their bilingual extensions so that they can teach in a formally designated class.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also, as my colleagues have mentioned, provide on-site coaching and professional development so that all teachers are equipped to support multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: ever their own language skills might be.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And I will just add on to that, the intentional strategy as we are expanding and working with community-based providers and also family child care providers is bringing in

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: educators who have very different linguistic assets and they're able to match their communities.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So that's a very intentional way of trying to ensure that we have educators who understand the multilingual backgrounds that our children are coming in with.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm always trying to get more parents to send their children to public school.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So one of the things that you're great at is what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What you're horrible at is telling people what you do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Horrible, horrible, horrible, horrible.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my suggestion would be, again, trying to think of ways.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm not a charter school supporter, I'll be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so I'm trying to get more students to go to your school.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So maybe you could do some information nicely laid out, not D-O-E laid out, and be able to tell people, because all Americans should speak two languages, every single one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But the question is, you have to tell people that you're teaching two languages.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because I have to tell you, if you ask the general public who doesn't have a child in the public schools, who's always complaining, they're going to say, we do not have dual language or anything.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So when you have that material, could you let me know?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks if the city is looking at dual-language models other than the 50-50 model. Branch says the current early childhood model is dual language but the division is open to expanding language access models.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks whether NYCPS is considering other dual-language models

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I wanted to ask about, just about very quickly about the dual language model.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know that you shared it's 50-50.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are there other models of dual language implementation that you all are looking at?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Or is this, I know...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Does this seem tried and true?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Within the early childhood program portfolios, our current model is dual language, but we're always

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: thinking about ways that we can expand language access to families who, under the umbrella term of bilingual education, thinking how that would look like for our littlest learners.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm glad you're open.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know we've got some folks here in the room that might have thoughts, so I hope you can stick around for the testimony.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether NYCPS or the state mandate language instruction in early childhood education. Branch says there are no state mandates in 3K and pre-K, but the division embeds multilingual support in its policy handbooks.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about language instruction requirements in ECE

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are there any requirements from NYCPS or the state about language instruction for early childhood education?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there specific requirements?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: When thinking about what we value most is ensuring that our teachers are equipped and prepared to support multilingual learners in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So specifically for early childhood education, all teachers are provided.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: with the professional learning cycles around supporting that type of language instruction.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That language instruction is embedded in the day-to-day, the instructional core, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So from the minute the child enters the classroom to the minute they leave, the instructional time that the teachers spend with the children are pretty much

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: overloaded, right, with language strategies such as repeated read-alouds, translanguaging, you know, supporting the home language and embedding it into the instructional academic outcomes of the child for that day.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Other strategies that our teachers employ, just to kind of name a couple, would include gestures and

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: thinking about like how we could accelerate their vocabulary acquisition by labeling some of the discovery centers or areas in the child's home language or partner language if it is a dual language setting.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: For a monolingual setting, those same strategies transfer over to support the students who are multilingual and sitting in those programs too.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Did you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But in terms of a state requirement in early childhood education, so in 3K programs, pre-K programs, unlike the K-12, where we do have state mandates, they do not exist in early childhood education.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: However, in the Division of Early Childhood Education, it is a commitment of ours.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we, in our policy handbooks for our CBOs, for our pre-K centers, all of the policy handbooks, it speaks to

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: ensuring that we are culturally responsive, that we are honoring home language, and that everyone's responsibility is to really to ensure that all multilingual learners are supported.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So the state may not, but the division, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks what parents can be told as the federal government pushes English-only policies. Liss says multilingual children will always be honored and that families can apply for early childhood programs in over 200 languages.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks what city can tell parents amid federal pressure

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Your flowers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is there just considering with the federal government's decisions on kind of like reining in, you know, executive order, making English the primary language, which just sounds, you know, insane to me.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What can we tell parents?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That want to enroll, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And like Gail says, I support her.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We want more of our students to like enroll in public education.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What can we tell them that feels more than like we have a commitment in our handbooks?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know that you guys, that it sounds like you're proving it, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Day to day in schools, but what can we do to codify that more?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How can we really lean into that in a more concrete way for parents?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I will just start by saying that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: No matter what stance our federal government takes, multilingual children will always be honored and valued in our early childhood system and our entire education system.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we will always prioritize ensuring that they can show up and learn in both their home language and in whatever other languages they might be learning in school and that we see multilingualism as an asset and a strength.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I think this is in, there are many ways in which we can codify this and the ways that we as an administration talk about early childhood education and our goal of providing culturally competent settings for every child, whatever that may mean to their family,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: as we continue to expand access to specific programming, really emphasizing and making clear to families, as we do today, when they browse their options for programs that they can

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: learn in a variety of languages, continuing to support families when they apply for early childhood education programs to do so in whatever language they are most comfortable speaking.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Families can apply to early childhood programs in over 200 languages and receive the support to do so today.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I think to Councilmember Brewer's point, we absolutely can continue to talk about multilingualism as an asset and to promote that, of course, to families whose children speak another language at home.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: and would therefore really benefit from that modeled instruction, but also to families like mine who do not speak another language at home and are opting into dual language programs because we see it as a value for our children to learn another language in a city like New York.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So in sort of both policy and in the ways we continue to talk about our programs, the way we engage with families and the way we speak as a city about our work, we will continue to emphasize the asset that multilingualism is.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez thanks the administration and confirms the locations of the new 3K dual-language programs. Phillips says one is in District 15 for Spanish and one is in District 31 for Russian.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez follows up on new 3K dual-language programs

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, we agree.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We will continue to make sure that teachers are supported in having linguistically representative programs, and we will continue to expand options.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And to answer your question earlier about those two 3K programs, one is in District 15, that is a Spanish-speaking program, and the other is in District 31, which is Russian-speaking.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, I have a follow-up there, but I want to just...

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether every K-5 dual-language program also offers a pre-K dual-language program. Liss says not every school does and describes exposure models that are not formal dual language.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks if K-5 dual-language schools offer pre-K dual language

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you, does every existing elementary K through five dual language program, do they also, if they have a pre-K, I mean, they should have a pre-K, do they also offer dual language, pre-K dual language?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Not every single one.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I will say, not to, again, generalize from my own experience, but my children go to an elementary school that has dual language Spanish beginning in kindergarten, though there is no formal dual language in the 3K and pre-K, different school than I was at last year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The school is emphasizing language exposure in the early childhood years, so there are ways in which children can be exposed in early childhood, even if it is not a formal dual language program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there a plan to, if they have these dual language programs existing, is there a plan?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And if we can't get there, what are some of those challenges?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But is there a plan to extend, yes, into 3K and even into 3K?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, we have.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We can get you the data on exactly how many of the existing kindergarten dual language have pre-K dual language.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And then the next piece that we have been collaborating really closely with, with Division of Early Childhood Education, is on examining the places that have kindergarten dual language and do not.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And have pre-K, but it's not dual language, if there's a community interest and how we can increase continuity in that way.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So it's something that we're actively looking at that data and using that to inform where new programs may be needed.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez describes her older daughter losing Spanish in a 3K program and her desire for more dual-language seats. She asks how NYCPS plans to expand and whether any districts lack dual-language programs.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez shares personal bilingual experience and asks about expansion

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm really encouraged by the 3K dual language programs that you just shared.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think as a parent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: who does speak more than one language at home, it is incredibly attractive to me to ensure that my child is exposed, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I think the transition, I'll just give you the example of my older daughter, where we spoke Spanish at home.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: She enrolled in a New York, an NYCPS 3K program, and it was wonderful for vocabulary, but no bueno for Espanol.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It really felt like she lost a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so then we intentionally kept her there so that we could enroll her in pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And it just felt, it felt like that was not happening across the district and District 32, for example, but really in all of my, in my council district.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So I'm really interested in wanting to ensure that, yes, we expand, getting all the things we need.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think the concern is obviously the pipeline for all things early childhood education, but obviously, especially if we're talking about immersion programs and dual language, there's a shortage.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I think it's really important for us to really spread the word that this is, this is a direction the city is moving in.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I don't, I don't know any parent who's enrolled there can do a language and regretted it, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so I think there's so much value there.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I hope that, I hope that we can do it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I hope that we can really like talk about investment to be able to expand.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are there...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Kind of how are you all looking at expansion for dual language programs?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know that you share kind of like the specific rubric, but just equity wise, are there school districts in New York City right now that don't have a single dual language program?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And kind of like if there is, how do you how do you plan to expand?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And yeah, how are you all looking to...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Continue to expand it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What do you need?

chapters.summary: Liss says many community-based organizations and family child care homes provide rich multilingual experiences. She says the city wants families to understand pathways from those settings into kindergarten.
chapters.title: Liss highlights community-based and family child care language pathways

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: First, I want to just say one thing in response to what you were just talking about in terms of the path for children to be able to articulate from program to program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then I'll turn to my colleagues to talk a little bit about expansion.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But do you want to just, of course, highlight, obviously, we're talking about schools and the continuity opportunity within schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also know that so many of our community-based organizations and family child care homes provide an incredibly rich multilingual experience for children.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And for many families, that may be where they are comfortable with their child attending early childhood education for a variety of reasons, including language access.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we certainly want to help families understand those pathways as well, that they can learn in their home language in a community-based program or a family child care setting and then articulate into kindergarten at their local elementary school.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So for families, the pathways may not necessarily mean staying in the same building, but certainly we want to make sure we are talking about all of our early childhood settings and the language opportunities within them.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But I'll pass to my colleagues to talk a bit more about future expansion.

chapters.summary: Branch says a current strategy is converting classrooms into dual-language programs and inviting schools to add classrooms. She says planning considers data, community demand, staffing, and continuity.
chapters.title: Branch explains converting classrooms into dual-language programs

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So thinking about ways that we, again, could provide our families with more access, one of our current strategies is to convert certain classrooms into dual language programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So what we're working towards with school leaders and districts and

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: is thinking about ways that we can invite, you know, schools that already have a dual language program to open up additional classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But like my colleague, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Garcia, suggested or shared, our offices work closely together so that there is this more intentional focus and look on what the data suggests and what we can do to now meet those gaps,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: specifically around making sure that if there is going to be an elementary school down the street that has

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: you know, a dual language program in Italian, thinking about ways that the local preschools, pre-K centers, family networks can kind of like offer those programs too, so that when the child continues through their,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: you know, education career, they have that solid continuity and foundation around their partner language that they have been engaging in since they were smaller.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And what is the, I guess just to your point about, you know, encouraging schools to open up new classrooms for the potential of dual language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What is, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I feel like my experience with the department regarding early childhood education, it feels like the data and the seat allotment don't match, you know, in my opinion, in some of these districts.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so how are you all looking?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like, what is the data that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like, how are you able to justify that or rectify that?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And are you in these scenarios?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you asking?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thinking about additional seats or having those schools potentially move seats from existing programs and switch them over to dual language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we look at that data and think about, you know, this is a good problem to have, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We've got the family demand, the seat numbers are what they are, and then the family demands are another sort of like data set.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So again, thinking about ways that we can intentionally support and expand those programs, but at the core of that work is always going to be around like family need and family, you know, requests.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And then thinking about what the supports would be like for that particular school, if there are going to be any needs around, you know, getting a certified bilingual teacher to teach that program.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Those are the things that we're considering.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And again, it's just more around factoring all of these different elements to make sure that when we do expand, it's intentional.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We don't want to expand for the sake of expanding.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We want to make sure it's done well and it's done right and it's sustained for years to come.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I mean, I understand it has to sort of feel like the perfect storm to have all of those things in motion.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether the classroom conversion strategy has succeeded in opening new dual-language classrooms. Branch says leaders are interested but no new classroom has opened yet.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks if conversion strategy has opened new classrooms

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Has that garnered any success in opening up new classrooms?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: The current strategy right now is to convert classrooms, and there are leaders who are 100% excited about it.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: My team and I have been on the field kind of just getting the interest ideas, the surveys around what schools and communities are already asking for.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And to answer your question, yeah, leaders are completely open to that strategy.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But we haven't started, we haven't opened up a new classroom.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez mentions One World Project's Spanish immersion program and asks how NYCPS works with existing providers. Branch describes bilingual education models including immersion, dual language, and transitional bilingual education.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about partnerships with One World Project

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So you referenced some of these, some other local providers that might be able to provide potential two-year-old, three-year-olds with some of these like multi-language experiences.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know that we have Joanne here from One World Project.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think I visited her site.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: If you haven't, DC, you should.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But it's really a really thoughtful and wonderful program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How are you all?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As you're thinking about potential expansion, how are you all working with a group like that that is already kind of doing this work?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is there a communication when, for example, a parent goes to a school where this just doesn't exist, they really want it, or they're just not equipped necessarily?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are there referrals to some of these providers in those instances?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: What I love about bilingual education is it's an umbrella with different models.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And one of the models that I know of that One World has is this Spanish immersion model, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So that's one model.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Then we've got the dual language model.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Then we've got transitional bilingual.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Those are different types of ways that we support students'home language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But to answer your question, if we're thinking about expansion, then that also includes thinking about expanding the different type of models that we offer to our families, too.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether dual language is the only model currently offered in early childhood. Branch confirms it is the main model, with One World Project as an immersion exception.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez confirms dual language is current ECE model

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And just to confirm, the...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Only model right now is the existing one that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Dual language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For dual language, yes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: With the exception of one world with immersion.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez says many private immersion programs are unaffordable and often offer languages like French or Japanese. She asks how the city will ensure equitable access to multilingual early childhood education.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez raises equity in paid immersion programs

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And on that, this will be my last question related to this topic.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know that, for example, in my district, there are a number of schools that offer immersion as well in other languages.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But in every instance, you know, parents are paying for this.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I know that there is an interest for many parents of all different sorts of income.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They want to enroll their child.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They just can't afford it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How are you all thinking about...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Expansion and ensuring equitable access to multilingual education in early childhood for all families.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because I feel like in some neighborhoods, this is where you'll see immersion programs that are usually not Spanish, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's like French or Japanese, you know?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But how can we ensure equity?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because I think parents...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Want to do that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And more than anything, they want to be able to ensure that their child is like learning another language, because like Gail said, we should we should already be doing that.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I think this is connected to just the focus on expanding child care options on, you know, addressing

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: of course, affordability broadly, but also making sure that we're providing programs that families want.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So we are intentional in working with community-based programs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: looking for opportunities where if we are able to expand, then we're able to work with more programs that might offer different types of dual language settings for young children.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: But I will just say, we know that there is a lot of demand and interest for different types of multilingual programs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And as you can hear from any of our responses, this is a priority for the chancellor, for the mayor, and making sure that we're working together across as many different options and making sure that principals and schools and superintendents,

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: if they hear of a need that we're working together to offer programs that the families are looking for.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And if I could just add, we also are very intentional with understanding that the purpose of bilingual education programs are, again, to support the multilingual learner.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And if we're thinking about expansion and what the community needs are, at the end of the day, it's what that community needs for the multilingual learner that lives in that community.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So if there's a significant population of students whose home language is Russian, then we're going to think about that when we're considering expansion.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: While monolingual learners benefit from those programs, multilingual learners depend on those programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So that's definitely.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: one of our driving markers around what we are looking for and when we're thinking about expansion.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: I want to make that kind of like, you know.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: No, excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how NYCPS ensures multilingual learners transition from pre-K to kindergarten without gaps in services. Garcia says identification can begin June 1 and includes home language surveys and assessments.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about pre-K to kindergarten transition gaps

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How does NYCPS ensure successful transition of a multilingual learner from pre-K to kindergarten, making sure there are no gaps in services?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So I spoke a little bit about this before.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: It does begin with the identification process.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And the fact that Part 154 allows us to begin the identification process in June 1st is really a game changer.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: That was not always the case because it opens that window to be able to bring in the family, do the home language survey, get to know the student, identify them.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And if they are, for the parent to make their decision, right, like to understand what they have at the school.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Given that in kindergarten, right, we have the NISATL, which does provide the language proficiency in English of the student.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And that's a good foundational, like, start to know where the child is in English proficiency.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We have a Spanish lab for all students who come in with home language of Spanish to get a sense of their Spanish language skills, right?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And then we have, you know, additional assessments that are done at the school level to get to know students, along with parent questionnaires to get to know the parent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how NYCPS meets both language and special education needs, including for children under and over three. Branch says CPSE evaluates in the home language and embeds bilingual services in IEPs.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about multilingual children with disabilities

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: If a multilingual child is also identified as disabled and in need of special education,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: services, how does NYCPS and Mayor's Office of Child Care ensure that they are meeting both those needs, and is it different when the child is three years old and eligible for EI

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: compared to when the child is over three years old and eligible for special education services?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: I could speak to what that looks like for early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools never wants to have a family make the decision between having their child choose from a language support or supports with their special education needs, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So what we have for our early childhood students is if a child is referred for special education services, our CPSC team,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: our committee for preschool special education team, then would administer the assessment or the questionnaire in that child's home language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And the rationale behind that is to ensure that if there is going to be an evaluation that comes out of that, that that evaluation may or may not necessarily need to be in that child's home language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So let's assume it is.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: If there is a cause for evaluation or a case for evaluation, the child's evaluation is done in that home language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And what happens is now we've got our own internal folks that go out and administer the evaluation, or sometimes we partner with outside agencies to support that work.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: If the...

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: designation is that the child will now have an IEP or individualized education plan, then those bilingual services are embedded into that child's IEP.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And what our CPSC team does now is work to ensure that those programs and services are rendered, and they work around the clock to make sure that there's continuity in those services too.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how many applications NYCPS receives for dual-language programs by target language. Branch reports 28 Russian and 60 Spanish 3K applicants, and 1,574 Spanish pre-K applicants among other languages.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez requests dual-language application counts

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I want to ask a question about, I think we kind of touched on this, but how many applications does NYCPS receive for dual language programs?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you have a breakdown of those applications by target language?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay, so we do have a breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So for 3K, we received 28 applicants for Russian, the language Russian, and 60 for Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So those are for the two 3K programs that we opened this year.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Now in terms of pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: 17 Arabic, 129 Chinese, 100 French, 47 Italian, 24 Korean, 34 Polish,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: 60 Russian, and 1,574 Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Wow.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's a lot of demand.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What are we doing?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We're not moving fast enough.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We're doing something right, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That too.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Oh, in terms of 3K, yes.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We're starting and, you know, we're looking at the data to see where and when we can expand 3K.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But the demand is there.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, clearly.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Families trust us and want their children in these programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we're excited about that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How long are...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How long have these pre-K dual language programs been in existence?

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how long pre-K dual-language programs have existed and what happens when enrollment declines. She cites a Japanese dual-language program that closed and asks how NYCPS supports schools.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about program longevity and enrollment decline

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I mean, it might all be different, but has it been like in the last five years or so?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: There are different, you know, there are programs that, you know,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: have been developed, I guess, you know, more recently, but the majority of them was definitely during the last expansion under the de Blasio administration.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And are there instances where in some of these dual language early childhood programs,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think of putting my parent hat on.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I want my daughter to be in a dual language Spanish program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I apply in a pre-K program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And for some reason in the third or fourth grade, it feels like it's falling apart.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That's not what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm giving you an example.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What does NYCPS do to support schools when maybe enrollment?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is dwindling.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I have a school in my district that had a Japanese dual language program, and I think they ultimately stopped.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like they just, the enrollment was very low.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I don't know if the support was fully there, but does, how often does that happen where these schools at some point just, maybe the dual language program is not really a fit?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And what do you do beforehand to support those schools so that they do keep it?

chapters.summary: Brenda Garcia says bilingual revitalization was created to prevent a revolving door of opening and closing programs. She says NYCPS has tight protocols before closure and has achieved net increases in bilingual programs.
chapters.title: Garcia explains program closure protocols and revitalization

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, you bring up a really, really important point.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So one of the things, one of the reasons we called our efforts for over the past few years bilingual revitalization was because we needed to

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: take stock of what existed, how they were being supported, and making sure that we didn't have like a revolving door of programs opening and closing.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And so we invested in that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Programs close for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We have tight protocols in the K-12 space in which if a program is going to close, if a principal either says we don't have the certified teacher or our parents aren't interested or we don't have enough students.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: They complete a protocol that's then submitted to superintendent and L director for review and sign off.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And ultimately, it comes to the Office of Multilingual Learners.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We do everything to try to save a program before closing it.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Like, really.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you have a sense of how many you've had to close?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We have annual data.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: I don't have it right now, but we can get it for you.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: What I can say is that over the past few years, because of bilingual revitalization, we've been able to have net increases in programs.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Because there was a time where we were opening up new programs, but programs were maybe closing as well.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: But now we're at a place where we're...

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: having a net increase.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So programs are being sustained, the existing ones, because we've been able to amp up the professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We've been able to ensure that if a teacher resigns, retires, that we have a pipeline and we're connecting principals with the right resources to get the teacher.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And at the Office of Multilingual Learners, we've been really

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: ramping up our efforts to increase access to home language arts materials, which is really critical to be able to develop, to deliver high quality instructional instruction.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: And so now I can say that we're moving from

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: bilingual revitalization efforts to boldly reimagining multilingual education because we're at a place where we are increasing programs and we have the mechanisms in place to really support schools and being able to sustain.

chapters.summary: Branch says neighborhoods change, so program planning must respond to current community demand. She says a former Japanese dual-language community may now need a different language program.
chapters.title: Branch explains geographic shifts in language demand

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: I want to just piggyback off of my colleague and thinking about

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: what I mentioned earlier, the different considerations when it comes down to how we expand a program, one of those being the geographic makeup.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So if we were going to, you know, based on your example, this community once had this robust Japanese dual language program, and now you're feeling like it's dwindling, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: If the family need or the demand isn't there, we got to consider our wonderful city neighborhoods change.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And if what was predominantly a Japanese neighborhood,

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: now has evolved into something else.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So then now we have to be responsive to that community and consider a dual language program that supports those families.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, I'll follow up about that individual school.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether there is demand for early childhood educators in a language the city cannot meet. Branch says current dual-language programs have enough teachers, though demand for classes exceeds supply.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks whether any language has unmet educator demand

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there a demand for early childhood educators that can provide instruction in a particular language that the city is currently unable to meet?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Of the many languages that you highlighted of what I think are the 3K and the pre-K programs, is there a shortage of teachers that can speak those languages?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Or that can instruct, excuse me, in those languages legally?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Across our current portfolio of dual language programs, no.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And the same applies for early childhood specifically?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Well, specifically for early childhood education.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So we're talking about our 2K, 3K, pre-K programs.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: There's no shortage.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is there, how do you feel about the...

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It's not specific to a specific language.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We do know that we have more demand than the classes that we have.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: However, it's not that there is a language that is being requested that we don't have.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: All right, that's good.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether schools receive additional funding for dual-language programs and the per-school average. Phillips says ECE funding is per-seat, with about $30 million supporting dual-language programs and no separate ECE language allocation.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about funding for dual-language programs

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do schools, and you spent some time kind of sharing with us how schools are supported when they take on a dual language program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do schools receive any additional funding specifically?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And if so, how much has been directly allocated to schools in this fiscal year?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And more or less, what is the average per school?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So for supporting our dual language learners and our emergent multilingual learners, we believe, again, that's a core responsibility for any of our programs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And so what they are using is their per seat allocation, and they have the flexibility to design their programs in the way that best meets their needs.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Best meets the children and the families in their program.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: For early childhood, there's no sort of designated or specific funding for, you know, additional things for dual language learners.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We are able to look at what the funding allocation is.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So for the dual language learning programs, it's about $30 million that is supporting the programs who are offering dual language learning.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I do believe there is additional funding.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: On the K-12 side.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And Dr.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Garcia, can you talk a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So I'm so sorry, before Dr.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Garcia, just to clarify, there's no additional funding specific for a pre-K program or the 3K dual language?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: No, it's based on the classrooms and their enrollment, not something specifically around the language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And have you, okay, and have you found that schools...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Need more funding for the dual language pre-K?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We find that the schools...

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Are they asking for it?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: are using, they have flexibility to, you know, support their instruction and their staffing.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: And it's something that we're continuing to, you know, monitor, listen to them and see how we can be responsive.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks what happens when a K-5 dual-language school wants a pre-K dual-language program. Garcia describes a $1.3 million bilingual revitalization allocation to 193 schools and $15,000 for new programs.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks how K-5 dual-language schools add pre-K

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And a K through five dual language school that wants a pre-K dual language, is the response from NYCPS?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you currently already have a teacher that can do this?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Or are there scenarios where the school wants it and they don't have it and they need more funding?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Branch, do you want to?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, I can speak a little bit to that.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So we have a school allocation memorandum for bilingual revitalization.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We just disseminated the one this year, about $1.3 million, went to 193 schools.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: Schools that are in the planning year and the first five years of program existence so that we continue to provide some fundings for them to be able to sustain.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: With that said, this is supplemental, right?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: It's not going to completely help a school stand up a whole program.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: It is for professional learning for teachers and for administrators, for parental engagement to get parents in and informed about the program, and for supplemental materials like home language libraries, home language supplies.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: We do include our pre-K programs in that school allocation memorandum.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So if a pre-K dual language program was to open, we would include it in this bilingual revitalization school allocation memorandum.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So this year, for example, any new program got $15,000.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: To support, again.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For any school?

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: No, for new dual, for K-12, it's any bilingual program.

utterances.speaker: Brenda Garcia
utterances.text: So dual language or transitional bilingual and specific to pre-K, any new pre-K dual language bilingual education program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, I might have some follow-ups on that.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether schools receive additional funding for multilingual learners in pre-K and 3K beyond dual-language programs. Phillips and Branch say funding is not language-specific, though programs can use funds for language access and instructional support.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about extra funding for multilingual learners

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And beyond dual language programs, do schools receive any additional funding support for multi-language learners in pre-K and 3K classes?

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: The question, do schools receive any additional support for multilingual learners?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's not a language program, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So, no, in pre-K and 3K programs, they are able to use the funding that they receive based on the enrollment in the age of the children.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: However, they deem in order to meet the needs of their multilingual children.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So they can use funding for translation, interpretation, for paying for staff who will be able to support the multilingual students'instruction.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: You know, and so we work with them to provide those resources and support.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And does the same apply to enhanced language support programs?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do CBOs receive any additional funding to support multilingual learners?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So there wouldn't be additional support for those programs because technically enhanced language supports, it's literally about the access, again, the language access for families.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So it's not an instructional model.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So because it's not a model.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's just ensuring that someone in the building can speak that language.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Anyone in the building, correct.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And there would be no additional, in the event where a parent is there and no one speaks that language, you're saying you don't need additional support because they can use what, language line or something?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: There is an interpretation line that they can call to provide them with additional support.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you, have you found that there are any...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Asks from schools and maybe like additional support or different support?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like, is there anything, and I know you've outlined specifically kind of what those existing supports look like, but have there been any schools that have engaged with you all on like, this isn't working, this is the way that we would want to be supported.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So not necessarily more funding, but like, we want to do this differently.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: We do get requests for additional support in terms of like instructional support, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: In terms of like additional strategies to help support multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And again, we're on the ground, so we're tailoring our coaching model to provide the just right support to those programs.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So yes, and then we are able to adjust and ensure that programs get the just right support.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks how the Mayor's Office will tap family child care providers, many of whom speak Spanish, to expand multilingual education. Liss and Phillips say family child care is central to 2K expansion and outreach is conducted in providers' languages.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about family child care multilingual educators

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think we're almost done with the questions, and so I'm excited to hear from the public.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Just maybe I think just two more questions, and I think you touched on it on some of the family child care networks that the majority of them speak another language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: In some of these surveys, I see that Spanish, the majority of them are speaking Spanish, for example.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How will the mayor's office tap into this resource to provide 2K, 3K, and pre-K multilingual education in Spanish?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So as we expand.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And are we going to compensate these people for this extra?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Gift of exposure and immersion to other languages.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So as we expand access to early care and education,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: in the city, we see our family child care educators as absolutely essential to that expansion because we know it is a setting that families often choose and prefer, especially for their youngest children.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know families often prefer family child care for a range of reasons, whether that's the intimacy of the program, the mixed age, the flexibility, and often it is for cultural and linguistic reasons.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know many parents feel comfortable knowing their child is in an environment that looks and feels like their home, whether that's the language exposure.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The meals they're eating, or just the cultures and customs that are practiced in that program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so as we continue to expand access to 2K, family child care educators are an absolutely critical part of that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We were thrilled this year with our first 2,000 2K seats to include a large number of family child care homes in that expansion.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And I'll turn to my colleagues, but we'll say that as we do that expansion work and as we do outreach to family child care educators to make sure they know about the opportunity to participate, it is critical.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we have been doing this outreach always with translation services directly in the languages that we know family child care educators are speaking and by partnering with networks who

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: do themselves have staff who speak the languages of the family child care providers in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: I would just add on to that.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It is incredibly important to our strategy to make sure that family child care providers are a part of.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: our early childhood system.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: We know that that is their, you know, one of their many superpowers is being able to reflect the children in the communities around them.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: It was a very large part of our 2K plans.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: They are also offering 3K from their family child care homes.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: So that will continue to be.

utterances.speaker: Erica Phillips
utterances.text: A significant part of our strategy as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think, I mean, I know folks in my community who intentionally will enroll their child in a family child care network because they want to expose their children to Spanish, for example.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so I think we're all saying the words that say we value them, and I just hope that we can make tangible efforts to really

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: show them that and to include them in the further expansion process because I think they deserve to really feel that value.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks what special efforts NYCPS and the Mayor's Office are taking to protect multilingual students and family data from federal oversight. Liss says the city will protect immigrant and multilingual students, and Branch describes FERPA and privacy protocols.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about protecting multilingual students' data

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And my last question, and I know, I mean, you responded on kind of our city's commitment to

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: doing what we do best, which is continuing to really push for diversity and not necessarily what the federal government wants us to do.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But just lastly on that, is there any special efforts that NYCPS or Mayor's Office of Child Care are taking to protect multilingual students?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Multilingual students and family data, special efforts to protect their data from any kind of federal oversight.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I'll just, again, reiterate the sort of broad value statement and then to my colleagues to talk about the particular data.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But, you know, whether it is this latest policy proposal from the federal government around Head Start, some of the other policy statements the federal government has made around

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: English and the stance towards immigrant students, we in New York City will always protect our immigrant students, our multilingual students, and they will always be safe in our education system.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That speaks to both their ability to be themselves, to speak their language, to learn in the language that they speak at home, and to have their information protected and kept safe.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But I'll turn to some of my colleagues on the specific policies.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: In my previous role as principal, what you just described is like a very real situation, like they happen, right?

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: But I do want to emphasize that what New York City Public Schools educators from

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: the crossing guard to, you know, the chancellor, our priority is to ensure that our students'privacy is protected and then we support the families that, you know, they come from.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: What New York City Public Schools has offered as specific guidance for what to do in that very real situation are clearly outlined as far as like what the protocols are when dealing with like non-local law enforcement or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: In addition to that, though, a lot of the language data that we collect for the purpose of instruction and meeting those instructional needs is not correlated or used for identifying a child's immigration status.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And with also this understanding that a multilingual learner may not be an immigrant and an immigrant may not be a multilingual learner, too.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So thinking about just the whole like ethos of like what that means for immigrant families.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: What also governs our day-to-day practices is the idea of, like, making sure that we are honoring and following the FERPA laws to the T.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: So those three different kind of, like, things that we consider when we're protecting our students is what kind of guides our day-to-day practice.

utterances.speaker: Georgette Branch
utterances.text: And if, for some reason, there's some kind of, like, back and forth engagement, we are advised, directed to deal with or get our next steps from legal counsel.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
