utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez thanks the administration and urges collaboration to expand and promote multilingual early childhood programs. She says she wants parents to know the city is investing in these programs and then opens public testimony.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez makes final call for collaboration and opens public testimony

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I am done with my questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just want to make a final plug to really let us know how we can help collaborate.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think it's such a value as I think we've all emphasized here today.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We want to make sure that not only are we kind of emphasizing this day-to-day for the existing programs, but sending a message to parents and all interested parents of NYCPS that this is something that

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: is in their local school district that we are investing in and that we do want to.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: expand again I think it makes it very attractive to parents and obviously our goal is to make sure that parents are sending their kids to our public schools.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So thank you all so much and now I want to open the hearing for public testimony.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez reminds the public that decorum is required, no recording is allowed from the witness table, and speakers have two minutes. She explains appearance slips, written testimony submission, and the 72-hour email deadline.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance slip with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez calls the first public panel, Emma Gossett from the NYC Independent Budget Office. Gossett prepares to testify.
chapters.title: Chair calls first public panel with IBO

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: First panel.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The first panel by themselves for right now is Emma Gossett from IBO, from NYC Independent Budget Office.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready.

chapters.summary: Emma Gossett of IBO says the office submitted public comment opposing proposed Head Start rule changes. She describes Head Start's role serving children birth through five and families in poverty, homelessness, foster care, or public benefits.
chapters.title: IBO's Emma Gossett introduces Head Start rule concerns

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Gutierrez and members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: I am Emma Gossett, lead budget and policy analyst at the New York City Independent Budget Office.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO is a nonpartisan independent government agency mandated by the New York City Charter, whose mission is to enhance public understanding of New York City's budget, public policy, and economy through independent analysis.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO has submitted a public comment to the federal government on proposed rule changes to Head Start programs.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: In my testimony, I will discuss potential impacts of these proposed changes, as well as share information on multi-language learners in early childhood education programs operated or contracted by New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Head Start is a federally funded early childhood education program.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: It serves children birth through five, as well as pregnant people.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Families are eligible if their income is at or below the federal poverty guidelines or if they are experiencing homelessness, are in foster care, or are receiving public benefits.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO's comment to the Federal Register expresses serious concerns and urges the withdrawal of the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO is concerned that the proposed regulation would introduce uncertainty and undermine implementation of Head Start programs that are critical to New York City families.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: In addition to providing child care, these programs increase families'access to resources that are crucial to their ability to afford and remain in New York City, including alleviation from food insecurity and increased access to dental, physical, and mental health care, as well as job training programs.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Over the past few years, New York City's Head Start programs have withstood major changes, including the closure of the regional office in New York.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Prior to 2025, New York City Public Schools served as the grant recipient for approximately 30% of Head Start programs in the city.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: But their grant was not renewed, and they will no longer oversee Head Start programs.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: In the 2024-2025 school year, the 150 New York City Head Start programs served 18,000 children, including 900 homeless students, over 600 students with IEPs, and approximately 30 foster children,

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: as well as over 580 pregnant women.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: These programs are run by highly trained staff and volunteers, who include over 1,400 staff members and over 800 parent volunteers.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: There are also other positions that employ New York City residents, which include home visitors and evaluators.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: I will now highlight a couple of the proposed changes.

chapters.summary: Gossett says HHS would require Head Start instruction only in English. She reports that 73% of New York City Head Start students were dual language learners in 2024-2025 and that many staff speak Spanish or other languages.
chapters.title: Gossett warns English-only mandate would harm Head Start

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: First, HHS would require all Head Start programs going forward to be taught in English and only English.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Head Start programs serve students who speak many languages, and its staff reflect this language diversity.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Additionally, families benefit from Head Start's language programming.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: In 2024 to 2025, 73% or 14,000 of New York City's enrolled Head Start students were dual language learners.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Students were equally as likely to speak English at home as they were likely to speak Spanish at home.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: About a quarter of Head Start staff spoke Spanish, and 35% of staff were proficient in a language other than English.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: And over 400 New York City families participated in an ESL training over the course of the year.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO supports the continuation of student language access and urges HHS to reconsider rescinding these requirements.

chapters.summary: Gossett says proposed changes would remove parent engagement and parent committee requirements. She notes Head Start relies on over 800 parent volunteers and that volunteering supports career development.
chapters.title: Gossett opposes removing Head Start parent engagement rules

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Secondly,

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: There are a set of proposed changes that would remove requirements for parent engagement and parent committees.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Head Start programs rely heavily on parent engagement and parent volunteers.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: In the 24-25 school year, Head Start programs served over 4,000 families, and single-parent households represented just under half of those families.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: New York City programs also hosted over 800 parent volunteers.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Parent volunteering serves as a crucial touchpoint not only to programs but to families, particularly those with limited supports.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Parents who volunteer have opportunities for career development through structured coaching.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO supports the continuation of parent committees and the continuation of strong parental engagement and urges ADHS to reconsider rescinding these requirements.

chapters.summary: Gossett says proposed rules would impact data and reporting and could constrain researchers' ability to study Head Start. IBO supports transparent data practices and continued data collection.
chapters.title: Gossett raises concerns about Head Start data reporting changes

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: A third set of rules that IBO highlighted in our comment would impact data and reporting and potentially constrain researchers'abilities to study Head Start's impacts and compare data before data.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: for and after those changes take place.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Um.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: IBO strongly supports comprehensive, transparent data practices and supports the continued collection of data measurements.

chapters.summary: Gossett says 31% of 3K students and 34% of pre-K students in NYCPS programs spoke a language other than English at home. Families spoke over 140 languages, led by Spanish, Chinese languages, Bengali, Russian, and Arabic.
chapters.title: Gossett presents NYCPS multilingual learner data

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Lastly, I will speak about multilingual learners within New York City public schools'early childhood programs.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Of the approximately 40,000 3K students and 60,000 pre-K students who were enrolled in a New York City public schools operated or contracted program,

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: 31% of 3K students and 34% of pre-K students spoke a language other than English at home.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Families served by those programs spoke over 140 different languages, but the five most common for both grades were Spanish, whose speakers made up 18% of all 3K and pre-K programs, followed by Chinese languages, Bengali, Russian, and Arabic.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: If proposed rule changes to Head Start are finalized, the families of New York City's multi-language learners may look to NYCPS for programs that support language diversity and access.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: NYCPS has an opportunity now to ensure there are sufficient resources for enrolled multi-language learners, as well as to build new supports for future students.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify, and I'm happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether conversations or plans are underway about the Head Start changes. Gossett says the rule is not final, public comments are due October 6, and families may seek NYCPS or private programs if English-only rules take effect.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez questions IBO on Head Start rule timing and impacts

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Emma.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And this is a really thorough and thoughtful testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I guess what I don't know if we heard directly from NYCPS on this specific Head Start changes, but do you know of any of these conversations or plans that are in motion?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: potentially considering, I mean, this is the whole purpose of the hearing today, really, is to understand the families, the student population, and to identify how we can better serve

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: or identify holes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But have some of these conversations started happening?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I mean, I think the 2-3K classrooms are great, but my God, it's 2-3K classrooms, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What can we be doing or what has started?

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Yeah, I think in terms of Head Start, the changes aren't finalized.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: So the proposed rules, public comments are accepted until October 6th for anyone interested.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: And so I think once if those are adopted and if those regulations come into effect, they may.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Impact the number of students who are seeking dual language programs, but I don't think that there are any currently because those changes aren't in place yet.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you, I mean, do you anticipate the same for just multi-language learners in, you know, if they do go into effect where...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They might be leading on an NYCPS program.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Yeah, I think if there are Head Start programs that stop using other languages, those families may look not only to NYCPS, but also to private programs if they can afford them, or family members who could care for them.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: And I think language is certainly...

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: A strength of Head Start, 73% of students speak another language in a Head Start program, which is, I mean, even higher than NYCPS.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: So

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: I think it's definitely an important part of the program, and there are certainly concerns.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And you mentioned the deadline for public comment is on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you just share on the record where people can share their public comment?

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Emma Gossett
utterances.text: On the Federal Register, if you look up proposed changes to Head Start, you'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, dear.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, I encourage everyone to submit a testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And thank you again so much for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Have a great day.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You too.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez calls Abigail Leonard, Raquel Grimilla, Karen Rogel, Albania Jimenez, and Judy Blumenthal to testify. She asks them to begin and work down the panel.
chapters.title: Chair calls next public panel of providers

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For our next panel, I want to call up Abigail Leonard, Raquel Grimilla, Karen Rogel, my apologies if I'm mispronouncing, Albania Jimenez, and Judy Blumenthal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Anybody can start when you all are ready?

chapters.summary: Karen Rogel represents City's First Readers, a partnership of 18 organizations. She describes play-based, culturally relevant early literacy programs and opposes English-only Head Start requirements.
chapters.title: Karen Rogel of City's First Readers testifies on multilingual early literacy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Gutierrez and colleagues for convening this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: New York is a sanctuary city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Our streets are filled with people speaking many languages, and so are our classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: But what happens before those children begin to receive formal instruction?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: I'm Karen Rogel, and I'm here representing City's First Readers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: The 18 partners of Cities First Readers deliver some of the most effective programs around to support multi-language learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: During the critical period from birth through five, that's the same time frame when children's brain grows 90% of its adult capacity, and that's the best time to engage a child with stimulation and experiences that lay the foundation for early literacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So how does CFR support multilingual learners and their families on the path to school readiness?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We focus on play and joy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We provide tools for parents to create safe and stable, nurturing relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: And that's what the American Academy of Pediatrics calls relational help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: And we also deliver free, high-quality, culturally relevant early learning programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Cities First readers approach is an emphasis of proposed changes at the federal level that would, if implemented, require instruction at Head Start programs to be provided only in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We value the languages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: cultures of multi-language learners and that bring to New York City and our programming supports them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So in closing, I want to leave you with two thoughts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: This is a real and powerful impact that comes from working together to support families with early childhood multi-language learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: CFR Partners operates in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: in a truly collaborative fashion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So I invite you to come see this for yourself by attending our quarterly meetings or any programs that we have coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: CFR is reaching out to non-traditional settings and establishing relationships with partners who are not conventionally considered educational.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Clinics, hospitals, healthcare providers, WIC centers, WIC offices, ACS family enrichment centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Early literacy supports must be a part of holistic process supporting growth, especially for our multi-language learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Albania Jimenez of Literacy in Community says a child's home language is a foundation for learning. She announces a Supporting Multilingual Homes workshop series and asks the council to invest in family literacy and educator training.
chapters.title: Albania Jimenez of Literacy in Community urges family-centered investment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: I think I...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: So good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: I'm Chair Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: I'm members of the subcommittee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: My name is Albania Jimenez, and I'm here on behalf of Literacy in Community, LINK.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: We work with children birth to five, their families and the educators and community partners who support them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: LINK is a facilitating agency for City's First Readers and Open Manhattan Early Childhood Connect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: A child's home language is a foundation for learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: When a caregiver sings to a baby, tells a story, or talks through the day in the language they know best, that child is building language connection and a sense of belonging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: Families should never feel they must stop using their home language to help their child learn English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: I just want to be specific on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: This November, Link plans to launch Supporting Multilingual Homes, a workshop series designed to help families build on every interaction,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: not sure their home languages, and share what they know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: About their children with educators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: Families cannot do this alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: Childhood educators

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: need practical training to learn about each child's languages, invite meaningful conversation, support home languages development, and intentionally build English skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: Families also need welcoming programs and resources they can use in the languages they speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: We ask the council to invest in family-centered early literacy programs and professional learning for educators who serve multilingual children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: Let's start before kindergarten and build on the strengths children and families already bring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Albania Jimenez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Raquel Grimilla, a Williamsburg grandmother and retired educator, urges continued funding for dual-language daycare. She praises Nuestros Niños and asks for music programs in public daycare settings.
chapters.title: Raquel Grimilla testifies on dual-language daycare and music programs

utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: I would like to address two topics, dual language daycare and music programs in daycare classes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: And I say music because music also is like a second language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Dual language daycare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: All daycares are a very necessary part of our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: In order for parents to work and provide for their families, they need a safe place for their children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Daycares provide enriched programs for children to play, socialize, and learn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Our daycares should not have to struggle for funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Staff members, like the staff members at Nuestros Niños, which is in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, which is a dual language daycare, they had teachers there that were not getting paid due to lack of funding, but still those teachers showed up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: As a grandmother, I'm grateful to Nuestro Niños Daycare for providing my granddaughter with a dual language program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: As a former educator myself, and I also was with bilingual, I was early childhood with a bilingual extension, but I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: I've been exposed to the research indicating that knowing two languages is not only helpful for learning about other cultures, but it's also beneficial to cognitive learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Dual language programs in our daycares give our children an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla

chapters.summary: Judy Blumenthal, Pedagogic Director of Early Starters USA, describes safe spaces for newly arrived families in shelters. She supports Resolution 650 and urges investment in community-based multilingual programs.
chapters.title: Judy Blumenthal of Early Starters USA describes trauma-informed language support

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez and members of the subcommittee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: My name is Judy Blumenthal, and I am the Pedagogic Director of Early Starters USA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We run early childhood safe spaces in four of the five boroughs for young children and caregivers, including newly arrived families living in New York City shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Through play, consistent relationships, and trauma-informed care, our educators help children feel safe, learn, and build resilience, supporting their school readiness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We also train mothers from the communities we serve to work in our spaces and pursue careers in early childhood education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Many of the children in our spaces only speak Spanish at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: When a young child enters a new setting, hearing a familiar language helps them feel safe, connect with an educator, and express what they need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: But language carries more than words.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: It carries a family's stories, traditions, and ways of caring for one another.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: When we speak with children and families in their home language, we learn what comforts a child, what they enjoy, and what matters to their family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We can bring that understanding into our work and show the children that their culture and heritage are welcomed and respected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Parents can ask questions and take part in their child's learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Children can build confidence in their home language while they begin to learn English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Chair Gutierrez, thank you for recognizing the importance of home language support in Resolution 650.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We fully support the resolution's opposition to the proposed English-only requirement for heads.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: What you describe is what we see in our spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Children learn best when their home language is valued, and we appreciate that none of this is new to you, Madam Chair, and that you emphasize and understand this issue better than most, being a bilingual mother yourself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Programs need multilingual educators, interpretation for families, and training that helps staff support young children across languages and culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Community organizations that already have trusted relationships with families can help the city reach children who might otherwise be missed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We urge the council and Mary Mom Dani to invest in community-based programs like ours that reach multilingual young children and their families, including families living in shelters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Every child deserves to be welcomed in a language they understand, with their culture and heritage respected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Every parent deserves to be a full partner in their child's early learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abigail Leonard of Children's Aid describes Head Start and Early Head Start programs serving 500 children. She says multilingual support is integral to Head Start and urges adoption of Resolution 650.
chapters.title: Abigail Leonard of Children's Aid supports Resolution 650

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Judy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez and members of the subcommittee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: My name is Abigail Leonard, and I am Policy and Communications Analyst at Children's Aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Children's Aid operates a comprehensive early childhood system across nine sites in Harlem, Washington Heights, the Bronx, and Staten Island, serving 800 children and families annually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Within that system, our Head Start and Early Head Start programs serve roughly 500 children and families through center-based and home-based services at eight of our sites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: As a Head Start provider, we know multilingual support is not an optional addition to early education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: It is integral to the comprehensive, family-centered Head Start model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Children's aid programs use a planned language approach to support dual language and bilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Our policy recognizes bilingualism and biliteracy as strengths and supports English acquisition alongside continued development of a child's home language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: When educators do not speak every language represented in a classroom, they use culturally and linguistically appropriate materials and evidence-based strategies to support learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: These practices are especially important in Head Start's family-centered model, but they also benefit children across the city's early childhood programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: A child learning English may understand a concept, but be unable to demonstrate that understanding in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Supporting their home language helps children participate, communicate, and build the foundation needed to acquire English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: It also helps staff distinguish between language differences and developmental concerns so children can receive appropriate support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: For these reasons, Children's Aid strongly supports Resolution 650.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: and its comments on the proposed federal rule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: The proposed rule would generally require Head Start education to be conducted solely in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: This would take essential tools away from Head Start educators and make it more difficult for providers to fulfill their statutory requirement under the Head Start Act to accommodate children learning English, prepare staff to meet their needs, and communicate with parents in a language they understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: We urge the council to adopt Resolution 650, call on the federal government to withdraw the English-only requirement, and continue strengthening access to multilingual early childhood education across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: We will also be submitting comments and would be happy to provide them to the council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez thanks the panel and asks what a dream scenario would require. Karen Rogel cites technology for program updates and more multilingual books, noting City's First Readers currently works in Spanish, English, Bengali, and Mandarin.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks providers about dream scenario and resources

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I have a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And thank you all, our friends over at Link, for consistently showing up to these hearings, but also I think just doing the work that you highlighted in your testimony, which is providing joy and making that connection for families.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think everything about the way that you operate is welcoming and encourages families to speak in their language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: in whatever language they speak at home.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's just about getting kids excited about reading and speaking.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know the council funds that City's First Reader, so shout out to the council members before us and certainly Speaker Mann and who continues to support us in funding it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What is a dream scenario for the providers where you all are doing things, we're all applauding, but you're unfortunately not able to do it unilaterally across the city?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Kind of what is the dream scenario?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What do you need to make that happen?

utterances.text: So much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: But we would like to invest in tech because our website is so very well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: If you go in there and just put your child's age and the community they are from, it gives them programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: But a lot of the partners do not have the support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We manually put it in.

utterances.text: Very quickly, just talk about the partners that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So the libraries automatically can't, it gets automatically updated because of the system they have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: And so does Link.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We started using Airtable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: But some of the smaller partners do not have access to that technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So the website cannot be updated automatically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We would have to like put it in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Another thing would be just more access to books and multi-language books.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: We work with four languages now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: But as you know, New York City has one of the most diverse.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What are the languages?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So right now the languages we work with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: It are Spanish, English, Bengali, and Mandarin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: And one of the partners is already working with Arabic and Russian, but there are so many other African languages or other languages that we would like to be able to provide materials and books in, and that alone is also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: expensive, the print and the ordering of books.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether City's First Readers is a formal NYCPS partner. Rogel says it is not, but it is working with New York City Reads Together to incorporate early childhood.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about NYC Reads Together partnership

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And just to confirm, at this point, you are not partners necessarily with NYCPS, like formal partners, correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: No, we are not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: I know you've spoken to Shari, so she's working with the New York City Reads Together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Yes, our DC is here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: I want her to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So New York City Reads Together, I know they are trying to incorporate the early childhood piece of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: So we are working with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: They're trying to work with the City's First Readers model.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, I support it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I think so many of our colleagues, we were joined briefly by Chair Dinowitz, who as well has been supporting this initiative for a long time.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks about the music program Grimilla mentioned. Grimilla says private daycares bring in music teachers and she wants similar weekly, biweekly, or monthly programs in public settings.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks Raquel Grimilla about music programs

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Miss Raquel, you said in your testimony that you were retired.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: There is nothing about you today that sounds retired in that testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But I do love that you highlighted music as a second language.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And did you work in West Los Niños or you just know them from the neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: I worked at PS250, which is in Williamsburg, Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: And no, I didn't work, my granddaughter goes to West Los Niños, but she had gone to a private daycare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: And they used to have a music, and I understand there are other private daycare programs where they have the music teacher come in and do like a weekly or biweekly or monthly activity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: And, you know, in the public sector, you know, we can't do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: It's kind of expensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Teachers aren't even getting paid, so we can't get, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: You know, hopefully things can get resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Raquel Grimilla
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And you're welcome back anytime.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Beautiful.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks Blumenthal what she wished she heard from the administration. Blumenthal cites language and bureaucracy barriers, plus fear among newly arrived families about sharing information.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks Judy Blumenthal what was missing from administration testimony

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then my question for you, Judy, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I guess my question to you, just hearing from the admin, was there anything that you, that you, her, didn't hear that you feel like were not?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Just based on kind of like the expansion potentially or, or how we need to show up for families.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Was there something that you didn't hear that you wish you would have heard or something that you love that you heard?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Um, I think that accessibility is, is certainly something that we run into our spaces are, uh,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: trauma-informed spaces for newly arrived families to the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: These families are, they will stay with us until they feel that they and their child are ready to move into the New York City programs, but like their understanding of the system of how to apply and how to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: navigate those programs and get into those programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: is not very straightforward for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: And that's speaking for the DOE as well as Head Start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: In terms of other things that I...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can I ask, when they feel like it's not accessible, is it specifically just a language barrier or just like, what does this all mean?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because obviously they're coming from different countries.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They don't do things the same way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: I think it's a language barrier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: I think there's also a level of a bureaucracy barrier maybe that's there for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: A lot of them are also, you know, in the political climate, feeling very hesitant to give information like their zip code and stuff like this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: So those tend to be the things that we run into when it comes to when we try to help them integrate into New York City spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: In terms of...

chapters.summary: Blumenthal says Early Starters USA has a workforce program with mothers and staff, partnered with CUNY and Bank Street College. She says the program has five CUNY apprenticeship slots and strong interest.
chapters.title: Blumenthal describes workforce development with CUNY and Bank Street

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: begun a workforce development program with our mothers and with our staff to help them find work in early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We're currently partnered with CUNY and with Bank Street College of Education.

utterances.text: Brief introduction into childhood development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: training with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: And we'd, you know, love to, yes, yeah, five slots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: So we'd love to be able to, you know, help provide those, you know, multi-link.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is that like the largest need for, or not need, but like, is that one of the larger interests for people at the, at your sites wanting to pursue a career in early childhood education?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We've seen a great interest from it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We've seen a fair amount of mothers want to sign up and our maestras who are our staff, they tend to, you know, want to see how far they can go in early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: So yeah, that interest is there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: You know, if they need multi-language learners in early childhood, please reach out to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: We absolutely need it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Blumenthal
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.text: This is really cool.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, the last budget, the administration and now the council's been able to fund, I think, close to three million, two and a half million to support this CUNY program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So we'll make sure to make that connection.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It would be great to really focus on that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks Leonard what she wished the administration had addressed. Leonard says Head Start providers should be partners in universal child care expansion and stresses distinguishing language barriers from developmental concerns.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks Abigail Leonard what she wanted from administration

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then, Abigail, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: My only question to you is, and I thank you for the support of the resolution, is there also, is there something that you didn't hear today that you wish you would have heard from the admin?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: I mean, we graciously appreciate what the admin is doing for multilingual learners and greatly appreciate the council making the point of where we can go further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: As a Head Start provider, though we currently, as was mentioned before, NYCPS doesn't provide Head Start programs at this point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Because of the contract non-renewal, we want to make sure that Head Start programs are a partner in the expansion of early education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: And especially as a program that is federally funded, there is a great incentive to being able to partner with our early educators in seeking universal child care expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that that is, you know, a central part of when we're considering what expanding child care looks like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: I think also that the point made about being able to distinguish between developmental concerns and language barriers is a point that we really, you know, we think a lot about at Head Start as a comprehensive services model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: We want to make sure that there is prioritization for children with learning disabilities and other disabilities, but also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: There is a big difference between a child unable to respond in a language that is not their native language and them struggling to be able to reach those developmental goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: So I think that that is a point that we are very concerned about for other provisions in the rule as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: But I think we want to make sure that that's a point that's emphasized.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, thank you all so much for testifying today.

chapters.summary: Betty Baez-Mello of Advocates for Children calls for multilingual outreach and better MySchools information. She reports that 65% of about 4,000 preschoolers with rights to bilingual services did not receive them in 2024-2025.
chapters.title: Betty Baez-Mello of Advocates for Children seeks bilingual special education fixes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Thank you for the chance to discuss the importance of supporting emergent multilingual learners and their families across the city's early childhood education programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: My name is Betty Baez-Mello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: I'm an attorney and the director of early childhood education at Advocates for Children of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: We appreciate that the city has committed to expanding early childhood care and education programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: As New York City public schools continues to grow 2K and strengthen existing programs like 3K and pre-K, it is crucial to support the thousands of young children and families in New York City who speak a language other than English in their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Among other things, the city should conduct more robust and targeted outreach in multiple languages to immigrant communities to encourage families to apply to 2K, 3K, and pre-K,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: helping ensure that families get the hand-on support and information they need to navigate the complicated application and registration processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Provide detailed information in the MySchools directories for families looking for programs that offer instruction and support in their home language, including specifying what enhanced language supports are available at each program and what that entails.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Increase efforts to ensure programs are using translation and interpretation tools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: to communicate with families in their preferred languages, and invest in additional dual-language pre-K programs and explore ways to age them down so that more children can receive bilingual instruction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: The city must also ensure that it is meeting its legal obligation to evaluate and serve young children with developmental delays or disabilities who speak languages other than English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Only about a third of preschoolers with disabilities receive their mandated bilingual programs and services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: According to data from New York City Public Schools, of the about 4,000 preschoolers who had a right to instruction and services in a language other than English

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: during the 2024-2025 school year, 65% did not receive the bilingual program and services they had a right to receive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: So as the city continues to make investments in early childhood education and considers ways to expand the workforce to create an early childhood education pipeline, it is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: crucial to address the need for bilingual evaluators, special education teachers, and service providers to meet the need of emerging multilingual learners with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: AFC also supports Resolution 650.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: And I'm happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joanne Derwin, executive director of One World Project, describes a Spanish immersion community center in Brooklyn. She says the universal pre-K contract leaves a $120,000 annual deficit and teachers earn about $25,000 less than public school teachers.
chapters.title: Joanne Derwin of One World Project describes funding deficits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Karen Rogel
utterances.text: Thank you, Betty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Joanna?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: Thanks so much for having me today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: My name is Joanne Derwin, and I'm the executive director of One World Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: We're a Spanish immersion community center based in Winter Terrace, Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: We were founded in 2012.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: Really started because I couldn't find a Spanish immersion program for my daughter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: And I did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: I just finished working at the Ford Foundation and I started an organization that built

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: collaboration between progressive business, labor, and community, and I was able to use my knowledge in nonprofit development to start a school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: I just wanted to emphasize how important it is to support multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: At One World Project, the greatest challenge for us has been about funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: So to respond to some of what the administration shared.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: Our current universal pre-K contract every year leaves us with a deficit of $120,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: It's incredibly hard to offer a high-quality universal pre-K program in New York City with the funding that is allocated by the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: The Department of Education does not provide our teachers with what they would earn at a public school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: It's about $25,000 per teacher in our school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: So we have to make up that difference by fundraising.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: So on October 18th, for example, we're going to make upcycled musical instruments and have a big waffle breakfast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: And everyone is making a donation to participate, and that's how we're doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: Little by little.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: trying to build enough funds so that we can continue to offer a high quality universal pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: So it's really frustrating to hear that those funds aren't available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: And just to close, we were offered a 3K spot, and we would have loved to be able to participate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: That happened a couple years ago, but it's impossible to sustain a school by signing another deficit contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: So I encourage the Department of Education to pay community-based organizations what it costs to run a high-quality program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: And I really want to thank Advocates for Children, which has been incredibly important to work with our families to secure providers who offer services in Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: It's incredibly hard to find speech therapists, physical therapists, occupational therapists, for example, who are able to speak Spanish to the children who are participating in our program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joanne Derwin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Joanne.

utterances.text: And I don't know if you were in the room, but I encouraged our new deputy chancellor to visit and to meet.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Who cares teachers, who care educators, who care, and parents who, like, know a really good

utterances.text: And you had raised the challenge it is to participate, that you want to be able to open it up to all kids who need it.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so I second so much of what you raised about what the city should be doing to really compensate.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Folks who want to get into early childhood education.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's very hard to promote a universal child care program when we currently don't have enough early childhood education teachers to fill those roles

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: or to inspire people to want to pursue a career in this sector if they don't know that they're going to be compensated.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I also just want to highlight for everybody, you operate a wonderful apprenticeship program as well, which I think is...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think we should be investing more in that with our CBOs because I think it's really special.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So no question, just my love.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you so much and appreciation.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks why so many preschoolers with disabilities lack mandated bilingual services. Baez-Mello calls for a larger bilingual special education and evaluation pipeline, citing a family waiting since April for a Bengali evaluation.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks Betty Baez-Mello about bilingual special education pipeline

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I did have a question for you, Betty, and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's disheartening to hear that there's still such a large population of families with preschoolers, with disabilities that are just not receiving the services.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I know that they exist.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So I'm having a hard time reconciling, like, why the number is so large.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What do you think, what do you think, what do we need to do?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What needs to happen?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What does outreach and communication need to look like for that to happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the main recommendation we're making today specific to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: children who need bilingual special education supports and services is really growing that pipeline and identifying the providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: As we've heard, it is really challenging for families to get bilingual supports like speech therapy in Spanish or for children who have more complex needs to get a special education classroom where they're learning in Spanish or their target language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: And so really think that we need to increase efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Across the board to get special education teachers and service providers, but especially ones that are able to provide bilingual support, and including for evaluations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we hear from families who wait weeks and months to secure an evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: We recently heard from a family who's been waiting since April because their child needs to be evaluated.

utterances.text: This is a special education evaluation?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello
utterances.text: In Bengali specifically.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Betty Baez-Mello

utterances.text: Okay, she's in the know.

summary: The Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education held an oversight hearing on supporting multilingual learners in early childhood programs and Resolution 650 opposing a federal English-only Head Start rule change.

Administration witnesses described NYCPS dual-language programs, emergent multilingual learner identification, family language access, educator pipelines, and funding constraints, while council members pressed on access, equity, and special education services.

Public witnesses from IBO, City's First Readers, Literacy in Community, Nuestros Niños, Early Starters USA, Children's Aid, Advocates for Children, and One World Project testified on Head Start, early literacy, bilingual special education, and CBO funding challenges.
title: Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education
topic: Oversight - Supporting Multi-Language Learners in Early Childhood Education Programs
